summary: regular pay is what the Overtime calculator works out, and it gets there from the regular work time, the overtime pay multiplier, the overtime hours and the total overtime pay. Think of it as a shortcut for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Overtime calculator work?
sections.html:
The Overtime calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports regular pay in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the regular work time, the overtime pay multiplier, the overtime hours and the total overtime pay.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Overtime calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Regular pay=overtime pay ÷ overtime pay multiplier
Overtime pay=total overtime pay ÷ overtime hours
Total regular pay=regular work time × regular pay
Total regular pay=-total overtime pay + total pay

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Regular work time = 40 hours, Overtime pay multiplier = 10 and Overtime pay = 10. The calculator returns Regular pay = 1 and Total regular pay = 40.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Regular pay = 1 and Total regular pay = 40 should be roughly the size you expected from Regular work time = 40 hours and Overtime pay multiplier = 10.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Overtime calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the regular work time, the overtime pay multiplier and the overtime hours — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Overtime calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns regular pay, derived from the regular work time, the overtime pay multiplier and the overtime hours. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Overtime calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the regular work time, the overtime pay multiplier, the overtime hours and the total overtime pay, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter regular pay in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Regular pay opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Regular pay = 1. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Overtime calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
